shortlist.raw_text: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138times while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

shortlist.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
shortlist.summary: The Cairn AI framework is proving to be a boon for defenders and attackers.
shortlist.raw_text: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system. “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said . shortlist.raw_text: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.

shortlist.raw_text: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.

shortlist.raw_text: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

Title: Anthropic's Claude Ship lets AI agents review, fix, and approve pull requests on their own

Text:
Anthropic has introduced Claude Ship, a new tool currently in beta that automatically reviews, corrects, and approves suggestions for code changes in accordance with team guidelines. The article Anthropic's Claude Ship lets AI agents review, fix, and approve pull requests on their own appeared first on The Decoder .

Article text (excerpt):
Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta, a new tool that automatically reviews proposed code changes, fixes problems, and approves merges based on team policies. The system pairs the already available Code Review feature for catching bugs with two new AI agents called PR Steward and Claude Approvals.
Code Review handles the analysis, while PR Steward steps in to rework the draft whenever tests fail, changes conflict, or reviewers leave correction notes, documenting every step along the way. Once that process wraps up, Claude Approvals checks a policy file stored in the project directory to decide whether the AI can approve a routine change on its own or whether a human still needs to sign off.
With GitHub auto-merge enabled and the right policy in place, new code can be merged entirely without human involvement, according to the documentation . The tool is available on the Team and Enterprise plans but billed separately based on token usage. Because PR Steward has no spending cap by default, teams can set their own budgets to keep costs in check. Organizations with specific data privacy requirements can't use the feature.

Coverage from InfoWorld: "Anthropic launches Claude Ship, extending AI-assisted development to pull request approvals"
Anthropic has launched Claude Ship in beta, letting software development teams delegate code approval to AI agents within limits set by individual repository policies.
The launch targets a potential bottleneck in AI-assisted software development, where the speed at which developers can generate code may outpace their ability to review it.
By combining automated reviews with the corrective work needed to prepare pull requests for approval, Anthropic is competing across a broader stretch of the software development lifecycle.
Its integration with Claude Code could make it particularly attractive to enterprises already using Anthropic’s coding tools , according to Lian Jye Su , chief analyst at Omdia.
But GitHub and GitLab have an advantage in how closely their AI tools integrate with their respective development platforms, said Deepika Giri , vice president of Asia/Pacific artificial intelligence platforms and advisory at IDC.
“Anthropic’s Claude Ship is not a breakthrough innovation as much as an evolution of existing AI-assisted code review capabilities,” said Nitish Tyagi , senior principal analyst at Gartner.
Claude Ship incorporates Anthropic’s generally available Code Review tool alongside PR Steward and Claude Approvals, both of which are in beta. Review depth is configurable at the repository level, with teams able to choose between Quick, Standard, and Deep reviews.
PR Steward handles corrective work on open pull requests, responding to review feedback and problems that arise during continuous integration (CI). Its remit includes resolving merge conflicts but excludes approving or merging changes.
Claude Approvals evaluates proposed changes against a policy file maintained within each repository. Engineering teams can authorize the agent to approve routine changes while reserving more sensitive decisions for human reviewers.
Teams can incorporate automated review findings into approval policies and define additional classification criteria in natural language.
Anthropic recommends that most customers initially run the agent in an observation-only mode before requiring its approval for code to be merged.
Running /ship in Claude Code initiates the workflow from the point at which a developer has a change ready for submission. Claude opens the pull request and begins working toward getting it ready to merge.

Background (Distributed version control, Wikipedia):
In software development, distributed version control is a form of version control in which the complete codebase, including its full history, is mirrored on every developer's computer. Compared to centralized version control, this enables automatic management branching and merging, speeds up most operations, improves the ability to work offline, and does not rely on a single location for backups. Git, the world's most popular version control system, is a distributed version control system.

Background (Code review, Wikipedia):
Code review is a software quality assurance activity in which one or more people examine the source code of a computer program, either after implementation or during the development process. The persons performing the checking, excluding the author, are called "reviewers". At least one reviewer must not be the code's author.

text:
Software teams can now let AI approve and merge its own code.

Anthropic's new Claude Ship tool fixes failing tests, resolves merge conflicts, and signs off on pull requests.

The mechanics are simpler than you think.

AI coding tools already write code fast. But human engineers still spend hours reviewing every submitted pull request, creating a real queue.

Claude Ship pairs three agents to close that loop:

• Code Review scans the code draft for bugs
• PR Steward fixes failing tests and resolves merge conflicts
• Claude Approvals checks a local policy file in the repository to decide if the change is safe

With GitHub auto-merge enabled, routine code can travel from draft to production without a human touching it.

Gartner analyst Nitish Tyagi called the tool an evolution of existing capabilities rather than a breakthrough, but the workflow shift is clear.

My read: the primary job of a senior developer is shifting from manually reading code to writing the precise policies that govern AI reviewers.

The limitations are clear. The PR Steward agent has no default spending cap, privacy requirements exclude some enterprise users, and Anthropic recommends starting in observation-only mode.

Would you trust software to approve code written by software?

Source: The Decoder, with reporting from InfoWorld and Mint on MSN
